{
  "need": "Competence",
  "secondary": { "name": "Status" },
  "read": "Tears signal that this student's sense of capability is fragile — correction feels like confirmation they are failing, not just improving. Underneath that is a status wound: being corrected in front of work they cared about feels like being seen as not good enough, which is humiliating even in private.",
  "pull": { "collapse": "Protector", "instinct": "Soften or withhold the real feedback to stop the tears — but that quietly tells the student their work isn't worth honest attention, which actually deepens the belief that they can't handle hard things." },
  "mentorMove": "Keep the standard exactly where it is, but frame every correction as evidence you take their growth seriously — not as a verdict on who they are. You are not protecting them by going easy; you are respecting them by being straight.",
  "holdFirm": [ "The feedback itself stays accurate and complete — no watering it down.", "The expectation that they engage with the note, not just receive it, stays in place." ],
  "stayFlexible": [ "How you deliver it: written margin notes first, then a conversation, so they have a moment before responding.", "Where you do it: a quieter corner or a brief one-on-one aside rather than in the middle of peer activity." ],
  "forceLevel": { "level": 1, "label": "Empathy" },
  "script": [
    { "phase": "Connection", "words": "Hey, I wanted to circle back on your draft for a second — do you have two minutes right now?" },
    { "phase": "Curiosity", "words": "When you get feedback on something you worked hard on, what does that feel like for you? I ask because I want to make sure the way I give notes is actually useful, not just landing wrong." },
    { "phase": "Collaboration", "words": "Here is what I am thinking: I am going to give you my honest read every time, because I think that is what actually helps you get better. If it ever feels like a lot in the moment, that is fine — you can sit with it, come back with questions, push back if you think I am wrong. The goal is a conversation, not a verdict." },
    { "phase": "Commitment", "words": "I want to be straight with you — I hold you to a high standard because I can see what you are capable of, and I would be doing you a disservice if I pulled my punches. The tears, the frustration, that is just your brain working hard on something that matters to you. That is actually a good sign, not a problem." }
  ],
  "longGame": "Over time, name small moments when they took a hard note and improved — make their growth visible and specific so competence stops feeling like a verdict they are waiting on and starts feeling like something they are actively building."
}
situation: A sensitive student tears up whenever I correct their work, and I find myself softening real feedback to avoid it.
